articles.title: D.C. May Abolish the Tip Credit—Again. This Time, the Minimum Wage Would Be $25.
articles.content:
In 2022, voters in Washington, D.C., opted to eliminate the District's tip wage credit—which allows businesses to pay restaurant servers and other tipped employees a lower hourly base that they supplement with gratuities. Known as Initiative 82, the ballot measure passed with over 70 percent support and promised to gradually raise the minimum wage for waiters until it matched D.C.'s traditional minimum wage.
On cue, the District suffered a host of deleterious economic consequences, prompting the city council to partially repeal Initiative 82 last year. Now, just over a year later, the campaign against D.C.'s tip credit is back.
The restaurant industry has long operated under a tipped-wage structure. As such, servers are legally allowed to receive a minimum wage below that of the traditional statutory minimum—so long as their tips make up the difference. (If they don't, the employer must rectify that.)
At the time of Initiative 82's repeal, waiters could be paid $5.35 an hour under D.C. law, with their tips making up the gap between that and the traditional $16.10 minimum. (D.C.'s minimum wage now sits at $18.40, due to inflation adjustments.) Initiative 82 sought to upend this structure by repealing the tip credit altogether and requiring servers in the district to be paid the full traditional statutory wage by 2027.
What happened next was sadly predictable. After Initiative 82's passage, full-service bar and restaurant jobs declined by 5 percent in D.C., while worker earnings fell by over $11 million as restaurants cut hours and staff. Surrounding counties in Virginia and Maryland endured declines of less than 1 percent during this same timeframe, providing a ready counterfactual by which to measure the negative impact of D.C.'s tip credit elimination. At the same time, many D.C. establishments began to add "service fees"—sometimes known as "auto-gratuity"—onto bills, thereby raising the cost of dining by a significant margin. Many D.C. tipped employees themselves have come out against the law.
In the face of this fallout, D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser called for the full repeal of Initiative 82; the D.C. Council ultimately settled on a partial reversal. This was a familiar story. In 2018, D.C. voters passed Initiative 77, which likewise sought to end the tip credit. Just a few months later, the council repealed it in full.
But just when it appeared that D.C.'s campaign against the tip credit was finally expiring, it sprang back to life. Now comes Initiative 87, which not only seeks to raise the District's minimum wage to $25 by 2029 but would also phase out the tip credit by 2031. Supporters of the initiative have delivered the requisite signatures to the D.C. Board of Elections, likely teeing up the initiative for an April 2027 District-wide vote.
The push is spearheaded by a New York–based organization known as One Fair Wage, which over the past few years has orchestrated a campaign to eliminate the tip credit in cities across America. As in D.C., this general effort has run into economic headwinds. A One Fair Wage effort in Chicago saw restaurants raise prices and cut staff hours, leading Chicago's City Council—a body not exactly known for fiscally conservative politics—to approve a temporary freeze on the tip credit's elimination.
Despite this clear negative track record, there's reason to think that Initiative 87 may survive in D.C., unlike its predecessor initiatives. That's because D.C. Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George has voiced support for scrapping the tip wage credit—distinguishing her from Bowser—even while expressing reservations about a top-line minimum wage increase to $25.
When it comes to eliminating the tip wage credit in D.C., the third time, unfortunately, may be the charm.

articles.title: Milei's Push To Privatize Companies Is Running Up Against Congressional Pushback
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
After winning the presidential election, Javier Milei maintained that "everything that can be in the hands of the private sector will be." That would be a striking change indeed in a country where the government, as of 2025, supervised about 60 "public companies." These bodies do not function as ordinary private businesses. They largely operate under special rules that generate monopolies, and the government absorbs their losses.
The Milei administration has explored several different approaches to rolling back state ownership. These include full privatization, partial privatization through the sale of shares, converting state enterprises into corporations as a preliminary step toward privatization, contracting with private companies to operate state-owned public services, and closure of enterprises deemed unviable. But the end goal is the same: a more open society where everyone can freely exercise their rights and be held responsible for their own decisions. In Milei's words, "The smaller the state, the greater the liberty."
The privatization process was initiated under the Ley Bases, a sweeping set of liberalizing reforms that, as Milei put it, aimed to "unleash the productive forces of Argentines." The legislation was instantly controversial, and Congress stripped out about two-thirds of its original articles before passing it in June 2024.
As a result, a plan to privatize more than 40 state enterprises was cut to just six companies of moderate importance. The law established a series of guiding principles for the privatization process, such as transparency, competition, and public disclosure.
The first privatization completed by the Milei government was that of Industrias Metalúrgicas Pescarmona, a metallurgical company. This was one of the less controversial sales—indeed, it wasn't listed in the law, because selling the state's shares didn't require congressional approval. It was finalized in February 2025, when the national government and the province of Mendoza transferred 85 percent of the shares to the American consortium ARC Energy. The sale price was $27 million, and the buyer assumed a significant outstanding debt.
With the Ley Bases in effect, the government got to work detaching itself fully or partially from the companies listed in the law. There was the Ferrocarril Belgrano Cargas, a train company; under the Milei plan, the state retains ownership of the tracks while private operators run the trains and logistics (and are required to allow other operators to use the network). There are the Corredores Viales, a group of road corridors, for which a privatization or concession scheme is planned. There is Energía Argentina, an energy company, where the government is divesting its assets and advancing toward partial or total privatization, among other ventures.
Milei hasn't stopped pushing for further privatizations, over and above the half-dozen enterprises listed in the Ley Bases.
Take the national bank—the Banco de la Nación Argentina. Like Argentina's other state-owned enterprises, this one is known for wastefulness and questionable employment practices. (In 2023, for example, it hired a numerologist to provide "coaching" sessions for staff—though courts didn't find criminal wrongdoing.) In January 2024, Milei announced his intention to privatize the bank. But it would first need to be converted into a corporation—a step the bank had described as necessary to open its capital to private investors. The courts blocked Milei's decree turning the bank into a corporation, arguing that only Congress can make that change.
Argentina's rail system has suffered for years from abysmal performance and service. And so Milei's government wants to privatize all the state railways, not just the Ferrocarril Belgrano Cargas. This won't necessarily mean selling the infrastructure, but it could involve separating assets and activities, selling rolling stock, or granting private concessions to operate lines, tracks, workshops, and services. Milei's minister of deregulation, Federico Sturzenegger, remarked two years ago that "by allowing free competition on the track, we free ourselves from the state but also from a monopoly contractor."
The president has also announced his intention to convert the government's television and radio operations—which he once called a "propaganda mechanism" for previous Peronist governments—into corporations and to sell, concede, or transfer their operations to the private sector.
Argentina's oil company, Yacimientos Petrolíferos Fiscales (YPF), has a special history. It was created as a state monopoly in 1922. Over the subsequent seven decades, the only private enterprises involved were some private concessions that operated on the YPF's behalf to cover its production shortfalls. The company often posted operating losses.
The YPF was privatized in the 1990s, and from that point on it achieved operating surpluses, generated exportable volumes, and delivered profits to its shareholders. But President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner renationalized the company in 2012, arguing that this would mean the "recovery of Argentina's hydrocarbon sovereignty." But, back in state hands, the YPF ran deficits again and was unable to supply the country with oil and gas.
The nationalization was carried out through the expropriation of 51 percent of the company's share capital from the Spanish company Repsol. Another 25 percent was already held by the Petersen Group, controlled by the Eskenazi family, which was close to the Kirchner government. It had bought that stake in 2008 and 2011 with bank loans and financing from Repsol itself, to be repaid from the YPF's own dividends. The arrangement raised serious suspicions of fraud.
The company's bylaws required that any change in the majority shareholder should trigger an offer to buy out the remaining shareholders. But the government failed to comply with this requirement, so the Petersen Group, which held 25 percent of the shares, initiated legal proceedings before U.S. courts claiming damages. This too stirred suspicions of fraud.
In 2023, a federal judge ordered Argentina to pay $16.1 billion but, in March 2026, the 2nd Circuit reversed, holding that Argentine law did not allow the damages claim. This has spared Argentina a big bill for now. The case isn't over yet, as the plaintiffs filed a petition on September 30 asking the U.S. Supreme Court to hear their appeal.
The oil company is probably the most significant operation to have been left off the Ley Bases privatization list. During his presidential campaign, Milei explained that the government won't be able to sell the YPF until it has corrected the company's financial position and increased its value. "In the energy transition we're contemplating, both ENARSA [another state-owned energy company] and YPF have a role. While their structures are rationalized, they're made to create value, so they can be sold in a way that's very beneficial for Argentines," Milei later added.
Under Milei, the company has indeed been reorganized, and it has made some significant investments. The YPF has now returned to profitability, and YPF shares listed on the New York Stock Exchange have posted sustained gains. But it won't be put up for sale anytime soon. Under federal law, any transfer of the expropriated shares that reduces the state's participation in the YPF below 51 percent requires the affirmative vote of two-thirds of both chambers of Congress—and Milei doesn't have that majority.
Echoing one of Kirchner's arguments for renationalizing the company, the opposition insists that privatizing the YPF raises a "sovereignty" issue. Axel Kicillof, the governor of Buenos Aires province and a presidential hopeful, has argued that "today more than ever we must defend our strategic resources and the role of the state. Privatizing isn't a synonym for efficiency, but for abandoning responsibilities."
And then there is Aerolíneas Argentinas, the Argentine airline. Privatized in the 1990s but never fully disentangled from the government, it was expropriated by Kirchner's administration in 2008. At that point, the Argentine state was already absorbing many of the company's operating costs.
During Alberto Fernández's presidency, the airline suffered heavy losses. During his presidential campaign, Javier Milei proposed transferring the state's shares to the workers, granting them a transitional period of state assistance for their operations, and eliminating contributions from the national treasury. "Aerolíneas has highly qualified staff and profitable business units," he later said. "It should be left to the employees. With more competition, the employees themselves will expel those who do politics instead of work."
In December 2023, Milei issued an executive order clearing the way to hand Aerolíneas Argentinas to its employees. But the handover never happened. After 13 strikes in nine months, the government declared air transport an essential service. A new decree declared the company "subject to privatization" and referred the decision to Congress.
Congress has yet to act, so the company cannot be privatized for now. But as with the YPF, the government has proceeded with the restructuring and normalization of the airline, which has ceased to run deficits.
Perhaps one day it will be able to do more than that. The legislature has blocked many of Milei's privatization plans, but he should be able to shed more state-owned enterprises if he is reelected in 2027 and if his party wins more seats in Congress.
During his inaugural speech in 2023, quoting economist Alberto Benegas Lynch Jr., the president called classical liberalism "the unrestricted respect for people's life project, based on the principle of nonaggression and in defense of the right to life, liberty, and property, whose fundamental institutions are private property, markets free of state intervention, free competition, the division of labor, and social cooperation." His attempts to roll back government ownership derive directly from those principles. Perhaps one day Argentina's oil production will again be in private hands, true competition will come to the railways, and the planes of Aerolíneas will belong to those who fly them. As much as Milei has achieved, there is a long way to go.
The post Milei's Push To Privatize Companies Is Running Up Against Congressional Pushback appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: The Absurd Overreach of Britain's New Porn Law
articles.content:
The U.K. has passed a sweeping ban on various types of pornography, with violators potentially getting jail time. This law isn't about child abuse or animal abuse or revenge porn, all of which were already criminalized. The new ban targets certain acts of lovemaking between consenting adults—which might, under a strict interpretation of the law, include blow jobs.
The Crime and Policing Bill, greenlit by Parliament in April and in force since November 6, bans pornographic roleplay that implies incest or an underage participant. (The age of consent in the U.K. is 16.) Strangulation and suffocation are also banned, and may be defined broadly enough to include facesitting. Having such forbidden erotica on your hard drive is now punishable by up to three years' incarceration, while "publication" (including sending it to someone else) can get you five years. Adult content providers and connoisseurs alike were warned they must delete any offending content.
In other words, watching a clip on your phone of a 26-year-old woman riding a man's face in a schoolgirl's outfit and calling him "daddy" could land you in a cell next to convicted murderers and rapists.
These restrictions "are far too vague and too intrusive into what consenting adults are allowed to enjoy," says Scottish sex worker Alice Mayflower. Although the bans don't fully apply to Scotland (yet), Scottish performers are very much affected regardless.
"We already have the Online Safety Act, so we all agree that it should only be adults accessing this content," says Mayflower. (The Online Safety Act limits minors' access to porn.) "With that in mind, what gives the government the right to decide what adults find sexually gratifying when the content is made safely, consensually, and by adults?"
The new restrictions follow a review of pornography regulations headed by Baroness Gabby Bertin of the Conservative Party. The review—which cited data that over a third of men stream steamy material at least once a week—expressed concerns that it may leave impressionable young minds with unhealthy and potentially dangerous ideas about sex, as well as promoting sexist attitudes. Notably, the review cited an anecdotal example of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.
Porn has "absolutely sort of normalized this kind of sexual violence," Bertin told BBC Radio 4. Bertin was also concerned that fake incest could be used as a cover for child abuse.
Nonconsensual strangulation (during sex or not) is already a crime, punishable by up to five years' imprisonment since 2022 as a separate domestic abuse offence. Although hard to prove, there nevertheless were around 700 convictions in the first year of the law.
While choking and other forms of breath-play can be dangerous, banning them means government intrusion into citizen's bedrooms (or BDSM dungeons).
The kink and fetish communities have been the most affected, and adult performers and their platforms have been busy scrubbing their catalogues of anything that might violate the law.
Some performers have lost hundreds of videos, which may not depict anything unlawful but were deleted out of caution anyway.
"I've personally removed 382 gigabytes of content from my PC and backup hard drives," says Mayflower. "Was I overly strict and removed more than I needed to? Probably. Was I willing to risk up to five years in jail if I was wrong? Absolutely not."
The law may actually go further beyond what most people think. The law defines suffocation as "depriving a person of air in a way that affects their ability to breathe."
"Any object inserted by another person into someone else's mouth could potentially affect their ability to breathe," notes Myles Jackman, a British lawyer specializing in porn and obscenity. "Under a strict interpretation of the law," he adds, that "could include fellatio."
In other words, blow jobs might just have been banned from British porn.
Ironically, the changes may push sex workers from online pleasure to in-person sex work, meeting clients face-to-face to compensate for the loss of earnings (paid sexual services, including the acts that now cannot be shown in porn, are not illegal under British law, although many aspects around it—like operating a brothel—are). That, Jackman says, could put them at greater "risk of being victims of male violence—when these prohibitions were framed around protecting women and girls from male violence."
Jackman traces the U.K.'s porn clampdown to 2005, when the Labour Party government began plotting to outlaw "violent" pornography. The Conservatives continued the cause from the 2010s, and now Labour has taken it up again.
In 2014, an update to earlier legislation effectively banned British-made porn that featured facesitting and other "life-threatening" acts (namely, fisting and strangulation), as well as "abusive" language and (simulated) nonconsensual activity. Unlike the new law, though, that law didn't apply to online erotica from abroad. At the time, hundreds of sex workers and their supporters assembled outside Parliament, laying yoga mats on the ground to sit (fully-clothed) on each other's faces while chanting "What do we want? Facesitting! When do we want it? Now!"
The rules were eventually relaxed five years later.
But in 2023 the Online Safety Act required visitors to the steamy corners of the web to either submit a selfie or present ID to prove their age. Since many people do not want their driver's licenses connected to their PornHub accounts, VPN use in Britain surged, with one app maker telling the BBC it had seen a 1,800 percent jump in downloads.
The government considered regulating or restricting VPNs before thankfully deciding against it this summer. It did call on platforms to provide more "robust" measures to stop underage visitors from using VPNs. It's unclear what exactly those measures may be.
How will the new ban be enforced? One of the largest porn platforms, OnlyFans, is based in the U.K. and therefore is an easy target for the authorities if it doesn't comply with removing content. Another possibility is that when someone is arrested for something else, the police will use that arrest as an excuse to check their devices and history.
Jackman is also alarmed about the British government's recent push for client-side scanning, which is when programs on your phone can proactively search for illicit content. This now includes facesitting videos.
"Jury trials that would normally have taken nine months to come to trial are now routinely being put back by three to four years," says Jackman. "So a decision on whether someone is guilty or not guilty for facesitting porn may not arrive for five years. And a successful acquittal would have no precedent value, because it is from a court of the first instance and not an appeals court, a court of appeal, or a Supreme Court. So, someone in possession of the same image could be tried in another court and convicted by a different jury."
The anti-porn legislation overcame minimal opposition from lawmakers. Indeed, some have even doubled down on their rhetoric, with Labour MP Jess Asato even describing oral sex as carcinogenic.
"Overall, very few people want to be seen as speaking up against the anti-choking, anti-incest and anti-[underage] portrayal laws," Mayflower says. But "if it's only 'perverts' and content creators upset about it, then it's easier to ignore us or talk over us."

articles.summary:
The U.K. has passed a sweeping ban on various types of pornography, with violators potentially getting jail time. This law isn't about child abuse or animal abuse or revenge porn, all of which were already criminalized. The new ban targets certain acts of lovemaking between consenting adults—which might, under a strict interpretation of the law, include blow jobs.

The Crime and Policing Bill, greenlit by Parliament in April and in force since November 6, bans pornographic roleplay that implies incest or an underage participant. (The age of consent in the U.K. is 16.) Strangulation and suffocation are also banned, and may be defined broadly enough to include facesitting. Having such forbidden erotica on your hard drive is now punishable by up to three years' incarceration, while "publication" (including sending it to someone else) can get you five years. Adult content providers and connoisseurs alike were warned they must delete any offending content.

In other words, watching a clip on your phone of a 26-year-old woman riding a man's face in a schoolgirl's outfit and calling him "daddy" could land you in a cell next to convicted murderers and rapists.

These restrictions "are far too vague and too intrusive into what consenting adults are allowed to enjoy," says Scottish sex worker Alice Mayflower. Although the bans don't fully apply to Scotland (yet), Scottish performers are very much affected regardless.

"We already have the Online Safety Act, so we all agree that it should only be adults accessing this content," says Mayflower. (The Online Safety Act limits minors' access to porn.) "With that in mind, what gives the government the right to decide what adults find sexually gratifying when the content is made safely, consensually, and by adults?"

The new restrictions follow a review of pornography regulations headed by Baroness Gabby Bertin of the Conservative Party. The review—which cited data  that over a third of men stream steamy material at least once a week—expressed concerns that it may leave impressionable young minds with unhealthy and potentially dangerous ideas about sex, as well as promoting sexist attitudes. Notably, the review cited an anecdotal example of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.

Porn has "absolutely sort of normalized this kind of sexual violence," Bertin told BBC Radio 4. Bertin was also concerned that fake incest could be used as a cover for child abuse.

Nonconsensual strangulation (during sex or not) is already a crime, punishable by up to five years' imprisonment since 2022 as a separate domestic abuse offence. Although hard to prove, there nevertheless were around 700 convictions in the first year of the law.

While choking and other forms of breath-play can be dangerous, banning them means government intrusion into citizen's bedrooms (or BDSM dungeons).

The kink and fetish communities have been the most affected, and adult performers and their platforms have been busy scrubbing their catalogues of anything that might violate the law.

Some performers have lost hundreds of videos, which may not depict anything unlawful but were deleted out of caution anyway.

"I've personally removed 382 gigabytes of content from my PC and backup hard drives," says Mayflower. "Was I overly strict and removed more than I needed to? Probably. Was I willing to risk up to five years in jail if I was wrong? Absolutely not."

The law may actually go further beyond what most people think. The law defines suffocation as "depriving a person of air in a way that affects their ability to breathe."

"Any object inserted by another person into someone else's mouth could potentially affect their ability to breathe," notes Myles Jackman, a British lawyer specializing in porn and obscenity. "Under a strict interpretation of the law," he adds, that "could include fellatio."

In other words, blow jobs might just have been banned from British porn.

Ironically, the changes may push sex workers from online pleasure to in-person sex work, meeting clients face-to-face to compensate for the loss of earnings (paid sexual services, including the acts that now cannot be shown in porn, are not illegal under British law, although many aspects around it—like operating a brothel—are). That, Jackman says, could put them at greater "risk of being victims of male violence—when these prohibitions were framed around protecting women and girls from male violence."

Jackman traces the U.K.'s porn clampdown to 2005, when the Labour Party government began plotting to outlaw "violent" pornography. The Conservatives continued the cause from  the 2010s, and now Labour has taken it up again.

In 2014, an update to earlier legislation effectively banned British-made porn that featured facesitting and other "life-threatening" acts (namely, fisting and strangulation), as well as "abusive" language and (simulated) nonconsensual activity. Unlike the new law, though, that law didn't apply to online erotica from abroad. At the time, hundreds of sex workers and their supporters assembled outside Parliament, laying yoga mats on the ground to sit (fully-clothed) on each other's faces while chanting "What do we want? Facesitting! When do we want it? Now!"

The rules were eventually relaxed five years later.

But in 2023 the Online Safety Act required visitors to the steamy corners of the web to either submit a selfie or present ID to prove their age. Since many people do not want their driver's licenses connected to their PornHub accounts, VPN use in Britain surged, with one app maker telling the BBC it had seen a 1,800 percent jump in downloads. 

The government considered regulating or restricting VPNs before thankfully deciding against it this summer. It did call on platforms to provide more "robust" measures to stop underage visitors from using VPNs. It's unclear what exactly those measures may be.

How will the new ban be enforced? One of the largest porn platforms, OnlyFans, is based in the U.K. and therefore is an easy target for the authorities if it doesn't comply with removing content. Another possibility is that when someone is arrested for something else, the police will use that arrest as an excuse to check their devices and history.

Jackman is also alarmed about the British government's recent push for client-side scanning, which is when programs on your phone can proactively search for illicit content. This now includes facesitting videos.

"Jury trials that would normally have taken nine months to come to trial are now routinely being put back by three to four years," says Jackman. "So a decision on whether someone is guilty or not guilty for facesitting porn may not arrive for five years. And a successful acquittal would have no precedent value, because it is from a court of the first instance and not an appeals court, a court of appeal, or a Supreme Court. So, someone in possession of the same image could be tried in another court and convicted by a different jury."

The anti-porn legislation overcame minimal opposition from lawmakers. Indeed, some have even doubled down on their rhetoric, with Labour MP Jess Asato even describing oral sex as carcinogenic.

"Overall, very few people want to be seen as speaking up against the anti-choking, anti-incest and anti-[underage] portrayal laws," Mayflower says. But "if it's only 'perverts' and content creators upset about it, then it's easier to ignore us or talk over us."
